attacksRun.attack: The D-163 anchor is stale cherry-picking that hides a later flip
attacksRun.evidence: This is the sharpest thing in the file and I pursued it hardest. Later successors do exist and they do flip the obligation: permission-leftover-join v3 and v4 both carry OBL-G09-HARNESS-SPEC at leftoverDesign false. Anchoring to v2 while a later version says otherwise could have been a way to keep an obligation open selectively, or conversely to look conservative while ignoring current state. It is neither, because the catalog discloses the situation rather than hiding it - the role text says in terms 'Later unrecorded successors are not this catalog's subject' - and because its claim is qualified exactly where it needs to be. It does not assert that OBL-G09-HARNESS-SPEC is open simpliciter; it asserts it 'remains leftover-design on the recorded join', which is true of v2 and is the only state a recording act has blessed.

observationsNotFindings: The qualifier 'as recorded at D-163' is doing real work and is the best thing in this artifact. Later successors v3 and v4 flip OBL-G09-HARNESS-SPEC to false, so an unqualified claim in either direction would have been wrong or misleading. The catalog instead scopes its statement to the recorded join, and discloses in the same breath that later unrecorded successors exist. That is the opposite of the defect class I have charged elsewhere in this sweep, where a carried-over claim went stale because nobody qualified it.

It is worth the coordinator seeing the split plainly: on the recorded state, OBL-G09-HARNESS-SPEC is open; on the current unrecorded head of that chain, it is closed. Two artifacts can both be honest and disagree about it, and the difference is entirely about whether a recording act has occurred. v3 and v4 also lack Codex counterparts, so neither is presently eligible for the dual-ACCEPT recording form D-163 used.

The FX-2A / FX-2B split is the detail most likely to be silently normalised to FX-2 by a catalog that summarised instead of quoting. It survives intact, and the fourteen-member count in the prose matches the fourteen entries in the list and the fourteen NOT-AUTHORED markers.

Live G09 v3 carries only namedCorpusNotAuthored, with no namedCorpusClasses, so unlike the G18 and G14 catalogs there is no exactByteIntent or passProperty available to quote. The catalog is complete relative to its source rather than thin, but a later fixture-authoring cycle will have less inherited boundary text to work from here than it does on G18 or G14.

decision.summaryForCoordinator: No blockers, no should-fix. The fourteen-member list equals live G09 v3 exactly, including the FX-2A / FX-2B split that a summarising catalog would have collapsed to FX-2, and the fourteen classes reproduce those ids and memberVerbatim values in order with fixtureBytes NOT-AUTHORED throughout. I swept for invented identifiers rather than reading the denials: the set of FX tokens in the file is exactly the fourteen with nothing beyond, and R-1, R-2, R-6, R-7, R-8 and R-10 occur zero times under a word-boundary pattern, so no refusal identifier is promoted into the corpus. FC-C1 and BLK-1..BLK-4 appear only as denial-list entries, and that refusal is well-founded since D-163 names OBL-FC-C1 among what remains on DR-105. The interesting part is the anchor. The catalog cites permission-leftover-join.v2 and qualifies its statement as 'on the recorded join', which matters because the later v3 and v4 both flip OBL-G09-HARNESS-SPEC to false. I checked whether that anchor is stale cherry-picking and it is not: v3 and v4 have zero mentions anywhere in COORD and no Codex counterpart, so neither is recorded nor presently eligible for the dual-ACCEPT form D-163 used, and the catalog discloses their existence in terms rather than hiding it. The qualifier is doing real work - the opposite of the stale-claim defects I have charged elsewhere in this sweep. Worth the coordinator seeing plainly: on the recorded state that obligation is open, on the unrecorded head of the chain it is closed, and the difference is entirely whether a recording act has occurred. The anchor pin is dual-reviewed and recorded, and neither pin is mine. 19 attacks run, 19 refuted.
